1.text: A street pup with caramel fur. Once it trusts its trainer, the tip of its tail lights a small steady flame that never burns the hand that pets it.

2.text: Guardian of the open-air markets. Embers freckle its back, and it keeps them like fleas that bite only thieves.

3.text: Legend says every caramel dog that saved a life returns as one of these. Its turquoise fire warms but never harms the innocent.

4.text: It never fully sleeps. One eye stays open over the nest, and its cry carries for kilometres.

5.text: After its first moult the feathers become iridescent dragonfly membranes. It hovers over water, hunting with surgical aim.

6.text: Four dragonfly wings carry a lean adult body. One beat throws a jet of water that splits tree trunks.

7.text: It drills bark for grubs with a beak still soft. It trains all day on dry stumps and comes home with a headache.

8.text: Its beak hardens into ironwood. It drums trunks in complex rhythms other of its kind read as messages.

9.text: Its beak has calcified into a granite wedge. It carves caves out of rock walls with blows that ring like bells.

10.text: Not one ant but a whole colony walking in the shape of a giant one. It scatters when threatened.

11.text: Queen of the leafcutters. She commands armies that strip whole trees bare in a single night.

12.text: It lives in riverside herds and lets anything ride on its back, tired trainers included.

13.text: Its huge beak is hollow and light. It swallows fruit whole and spits the seed 40 metres. It plants forests alone.

14.text: It steals anything that shines. Trainers learn early to keep their badges at the bottom of the bag.

15.text: Elder of its troop. It reads the future in river reflections and calls rain a week ahead.

16.text: It appears after wildfires. Its body is a serpent of blue flame that devours whoever sets the forest alight.

17.text: Its feet point backwards. It confuses hunters by leaving tracks that lead deeper into the woods.

18.text: The true lord of the forest. Where it steps, a century-old tree sprouts in a single night.

19.text: It charms fishermen with a song. Whoever follows it into the river joins its court forever.

20.text: It has only one leg and travels inside whirlwinds. It delights in dousing campfires and freeing caught POKéMON.

21.text: It survives months without rain. Its spines hold drops of sweet venom that draw BUG POKéMON in.

22.text: Whole swarms chase trainers for days. The only escape is a river, and hoping nothing worse waits there.

23.text: The jaguar of the region. It hunts in total silence, and trainers notice only once they are already down.

24.text: Its claws cut steel. It laps up whole colonies, but avoids the queens; it lost its tongue to one once.

25.text: Born grey, it turns pink as it gains confidence. It plays with bubbles it blows itself.

26.text: It travels in pods after dark. Folklore says it becomes a young man at riverside dances.

27.text: A white hat hides the blowhole on its head. It charms girls and vanishes into the river at dawn.

28.text: It curls into a ball the size of an orange and rolls downhill to escape. The dry scrub of the caatinga is full of slopes it can use.

29.text: Its shell turns to steel when threatened, bouncing physical attacks back.

30.text: It digs twenty metres of tunnel a night. Whole villages have sunk into its galleries.

31.text: It mimics any sound it hears, including trainers yelling as they fall down the bank.

32.text: Its red feathers throw sparks when it beats its wings hard. Flocks cross the wetlands at sunset in a long line of red.

33.text: It flies among the savanna clouds. The feathers it drops set the dry grass alight.

34.text: It floats with only its eyes above water, passing for a drifting log. Whole nurseries line the shallow channels in the dry season.

35.text: It waits for hours without moving, then drags its prey under in a single roll. It rules a stretch of wetland and tolerates no rival on it.

36.text: A direct descendant of the dinosaurs. Its jaws crack armoured shells. Only a handful still live, in the oldest channels of the marsh.

37.text: It moves so slowly that moss grows in its fur and insects move in. It comes down from the canopy once a week, and no faster.

38.text: It sleeps twenty hours a day and foresees rain weeks ahead in its dreams. Farmers in the coastal forest watch it to know when to sow.

39.text: The size of an elephant. It walks once a moon and knows where every old tree will rise.

40.text: It learns to repeat words in three days, and swearing in one afternoon. It nests in hollow trunks high in the Atlantic forest.

41.text: It memorises whole conversations and repeats them to the wrong people. More than one secret in Arauna has got out this way.

42.text: It lives 200 years, holding the secrets of generations of trainers in memory. Elders visit it to ask what their grandparents once said.

43.text: Striped like a small boar. Its short trunk smells fruit 100 metres off. It follows its mother along the same trails for a whole year.

44.text: It crosses whole rivers submerged and eats forty kilos of leaves a day. The seeds it swallows sprout wherever it walks.

45.text: Spirit of the forest. It guides lost trainers back to the treeline. It is seen only where the rainforest has never been cut.

46.text: It is born two metres long and coils in branches waiting for prey. It hunts in the flooded margins where the current runs slow.

47.text: It smothers its prey and swallows it whole, growing on river legends for years.

48.text: The Great Snake of Amazonian myth. Its eyes shine like boat lamps on a dark creek, and legend says its passing carves new rivers.

49.text: It eats nettle leaves without being poisoned, storing the venom in its skin. It spends its whole larval life on a single nettle bush.

50.text: An iridescent cocoon that mirrors the blue of the sky. It cannot move, but it shocks anything that touches it.

51.text: Its wings are the size of human hands. The blue scales become a healing dust. Healers gather that dust all through the coastal forest.

52.text: Its legs are absurdly long. It gallops across the savanna after fruit. It hunts alone across the savanna, never in a pack.

53.text: It howls at dusk. It eats a sweet wolf-fruit and plants the forest with its droppings.

54.text: It appears on moonless nights, and its paws leave prints of live coal. Travellers leave fruit out on the trail to keep it friendly.

55.text: It swims slowly at its mother's side and cries like an infant when it gets lost. Mother and calf stay together for two full years.

56.text: A peaceful herbivore. It eats fifty kilos of water plants a day. It grazes the flooded meadows along the rainforest rivers.

57.text: Protector of the rivers. Folklore says it nursed the children who were lost on the water, and that it still answers a cry from the bank.

58.text: Its whiskers hunt for food in the mud below. It is nearly blind. It rests by day under sunken logs and feeds through the night.

59.text: Venomous spines line its fins. One prick costs you days of sleep. River fishermen handle it only with a folded cloth.

60.text: As long as a man is tall. It swims in the absolute dark of the riverbed. It never once rises to the light in all its long life.

61.text: It learns to use branches as tools while still young, and robs camps for food. Troops work the same stretch of forest for generations.

62.text: It cracks nuts with stones and has taught the technique to its young for generations.

63.text: Held to be the cleverest primate in Arauna. It solves puzzles built for humans.

64.text: It weaves webs in dry branches and eats the smaller ants. The dry season of the savanna is its best hunting.

65.text: Its stinging hairs cause an unbearable itch on contact. It flicks those hairs off its back at anything coming near.

66.text: The size of a dinner plate. Its fangs go through leather gloves. It waits at the mouth of a burrow the whole night through.

67.text: It mews like a house cat but lets nobody near it. It is born in a hollow trunk and stays hidden there for months.

68.text: It hunts birds in the dead of night. Its eyes flash green in torchlight. It keeps to the deepest parts of the coastal forest.

69.text: Rosettes like a jaguar in miniature. It climbs trees after monkeys. A single one patrols a range of many kilometres.

70.text: It buries nuts and forgets where. It plants the forest by accident. Half the trees of the Atlantic forest were planted this way.

71.text: It gnaws anything. Its teeth grow for its whole life. It cracks nuts nothing else in the forest can open.

72.text: It comes out only at night, running and whistling through the dark woods. Its whistle carries far enough to be mistaken for a person.

73.text: Its bite hurts like a full day of cramp. The locals call it the bullet ant. A single nest holds thousands, high in a rainforest trunk.

74.text: An aggressive swarm. It chases a threat for kilometres. Its paper nest hangs from a branch over the savanna trails.

75.text: It has no sting. Its sweet honey is used to bring hurt POKéMON round. Every village in the cerrado keeps a hive of them.

76.text: Bands of fifteen walk the trails, digging through packs for biscuits. The band moves as one, and no pack on the trail is safe.

77.text: It has learned to open tent zips and steals anything that shines. Camps in the coastal forest hang their food from a rope.

78.text: It lives in dark caves, its very long snout built for hunting bats. It has lived underground so long its eyes have nearly gone.

79.text: It releases a sickening smell when threatened. Trainers flee before it does.

80.text: Its spray of stench carries three metres and lasts weeks in clothing. It stamps out a warning first. Almost nobody takes it.

81.text: It plays dead for hours when threatened. It has fooled even the jaguars. It carries its young on its back while it plays the trick.

82.text: Its coloured beak calls to females from far off. It eats wild fruit. It nests in a hollow so tight it must fold its tail to fit.

83.text: It flies in bands of six, all feeding from the same fruit at once. A band roosts together in the same hollow every night.

84.text: Its shrill cry greets the dawn. Every farm in Arauna resents it. It patrols the wetland pastures on foot, calling all the while.

85.text: It swims in shoals and changes once its legs come in. Whole shoals fill the still pools after the first rains.

86.text: Glands behind its eyes ooze a white venom. Never lick one. It sits under the village lamps all night eating what falls.

87.text: The size of a football. It eats biting flies by the thousand. It swallows anything that fits in its mouth, and often regrets it.

88.text: It runs on two legs when startled, dropping its tail to throw off pursuit. The tail grows back over months, shorter each time.

89.text: It eats anything: fruit, eggs, small animals, even venomous snakes. It suns itself on the savanna roads and refuses to move.

90.text: It shifts colour to match its surroundings, and its mood shifts as fast.

91.text: It sleeps upside down, gripping the roof of the cave. A colony of thousands shares a single ceiling.

92.text: It sees with sound, flying in total darkness without touching a thing. It leaves the cave in one long column at dusk.

93.text: It drinks from sleeping mammals. Long company leaves its keeper anaemic. It shares a meal with any colony mate that failed to feed.

94.text: It stands on a single leg most of the time and topples in a strong wind. The wetland shallows are its whole world for the first year.

95.text: The great bird of the wetlands. Its huge bill takes a fish in one stab. It nests on a platform of sticks that grows for decades.

96.text: Pink from a diet of shellfish. Its bill is shaped like a spoon. It sweeps the shallows side to side without ever looking down.

97.text: An innocent foal. Nothing about it hints at what it becomes. It grazes the savanna edges alongside the farm horses.

98.text: It gallops faster than a horse, and its bray is frightening. It refuses a load it judges unfair, and cannot be moved.

99.text: Fire pours from its neck where a head should be. It walks on Fridays. Nobody in the backlands travels those roads on a Friday night.

100.text: The spirit of an entire mountain. Forest breathes on its back. Cloud sits on its shoulders for weeks at a time.

101.text: Its pointed antlers are still growing. It clears bushes with ease. It follows the herd along the dry riverbeds.

102.text: Its antlers branch with age. It eats cactus without hurting itself. It goes months without drinking, taking water from the plants.

103.text: Antlers so wide it must lift its head to pass through the woods. Old trails through the woods are worn to its exact height.

104.text: A water spirit in human shape. It swims like a fish. It plays in the shallows and copies the children it sees.

105.text: It pulls canoes under when fishermen disrespect the river. Fishermen leave an offering on the bank before setting out.

106.text: A bird that robs the rich and feeds the poor, or so the backlands say. It nests deep in the thorn scrub where nobody can follow.

107.text: It commands lightning. Its twin-bladed axe throws sparks as it falls. Its judgement falls on the mountain villages in a storm.

108.text: Goddess of the oceans. A procession of lesser sea spirits follows it along the coast every February.

109.text: Queen of the fresh waters. Its hair of wet gold runs on for ever, and every spring in Arauna rises from it.

110.text: The divine smith. It forged the blades that cut the souls of wrongdoers, and its forge still burns somewhere in the hills.

111.text: Its long mane streams in the wind. It learns to gallop in a week. It is born on the open grassland and never sees a fence.

112.text: It runs at 60 km/h for hours. The herders of Arauna tamed it. A herder and its mount work the pampas as one animal.

113.text: The great hump already shows in the calf, which is still unsure on its feet. The herd shelters it in the middle when a storm comes.

114.text: Its huge hump lets it bear the savanna heat without tiring. A single one can graze a whole pasture flat in a season.

115.text: Thick wool against the highland cold. Extremely docile. Its wool is spun into the blankets of the highland farms.

116.text: It climbs impossible slopes and eats dry branches. It is the only livestock that thrives in the driest backlands.

117.text: The rattle on its tail is still small. It learns to sound it slowly. It practises the sound for hours in the shade of a rock.

118.text: Its neurotoxin is already at full strength, and the rattle warns predators off.

119.text: One bite paralyses even a jaguar. The rattle carries 100 metres. It takes the warm scrub roads at dusk and stays there.

120.text: It hides among fallen leaves and gives no warning before it strikes. It is the reason nobody walks the forest floor barefoot.

121.text: Born at 30 cm, it grows a metre a year in a well-fed river. The male guards the whole brood in its mouth for weeks.

122.text: Up to three metres long. It breathes surface air like a mammal. It must surface every twenty minutes or it drowns.

123.text: It attacks in shoals, stripping a cow to the bone in minutes. In the dry season, a trapped pool turns dangerous overnight.

124.text: It eats fruit falling into the flooded forest, grinding seeds with its teeth. It waits under the fruit trees for the flood to reach them.

125.text: It leaps two metres clear of the water to take insects off branches. It watches the branches from below, tracking a beetle for minutes.

126.text: It discharges 600 volts, paralysing anything that touches the water. Villages teach their children never to wade the river at night.

127.text: It swims in vast shoals, migrating upriver to spawn. The whole shoal climbs the rapids together, and most never return.

128.text: It waits among sunken leaves. Its sharp teeth lock onto prey. Once those jaws close, nothing makes it let go.

129.text: It leaps up waterfalls. Its golden scales shine like coins. Anglers come from across Arauna for one fight with it.

130.text: The eyespot on its tail wards off predators. It attacks anything entering its water.

131.text: Human-looking teeth grind nuts. Swimmers find it unsettling. It waits below the trees for nuts to drop into the water.

132.text: Dark shoals slide through the rapids. A popular sporting catch. It runs the fastest water and feeds on what the current brings.

133.text: Gold stripes run down its sides. It eats whatever falls in. It follows the boats, taking whatever is thrown overboard.

134.text: Hard plates cover its body. It scrapes algae from the glass. It clings to one rock in the current and never lets go.

135.text: A brightly coloured disc. It raises its young on mucus from its own skin. Both parents feed the fry that way through their first weeks.

136.text: Its tail lights only when it is frightened, showing paths through the woods.

137.text: Coded flashes call to females. It lights five metres around it. On the right night the whole forest edge flickers at once.

138.text: It lives seven years underground before it takes its adult form. It emerges by the million in a single week.

139.text: Its song reaches 100 decibels. It is the sound of summer in Arauna. Whole groves of them drown out conversation at midday.

140.text: Its scythes are still small but already sharp. It eats ants. It waits motionless on a grass stem for hours at a time.

141.text: It prays before beheading its prey. The female eats the male after mating. It turns its head to follow anything that moves.

142.text: A translucent sting on its tail. One prick costs you a night's sleep. It hides in boots and under stones through the hot day.

143.text: Its claws crush beetles. Its sting can drop a full-grown horse. Every house in the backlands shakes out its shoes first.

144.text: A spiral shell marked with folk patterns. It eats greens from the bank. It leaves a wet trail along the riverbank all night.

145.text: It rolls into a ball when threatened, giving off a bitter almond smell. It works the leaf litter, turning dead wood into soil.

146.text: It survives anything: radiation, poison, a thrown sandal. It has outlived every attempt to be rid of it.

147.text: It jumps thirty times its own length and plays music with its legs. Its first notes are ragged, and get better all season.

148.text: Its song runs all night without a break, and announces rain. Farmers listen for it before deciding when to plant.

149.text: It raises its front legs before it strikes. Its venom attacks the nerves. It hides in banana bunches and in boots left outside.

150.text: It hunts spiders the size of hands and drags them back to the nest. It paralyses the spider first and keeps it alive for the grubs.

151.text: Its sting hurts for hours. It builds mud nests under roof tiles. The mud nest hardens like stone in a single hot day.

152.text: It eats furniture from the inside. You only notice when it collapses. Whole houses in the old quarters have gone that way.

153.text: It lives thirty years, laying without pause. The whole mound grows up around it, and the colony never lets it move.

154.text: Its huge jaws guard the queen. It does not feed, only fight. It starves rather than leave the tunnel it was set to hold.

155.text: It marches in single file for kilometres, devouring all in its path. A column can take three hours to pass a single point.

156.text: It beats its wings eighty times a second and flies backwards or upside down. It must feed every ten minutes or it starves.

157.text: Its song is held the finest in the land, and it announces the spring. Every yard in the coastal forest wakes to it.

158.text: It shouts its own name, telling the whole yard whatever it has seen. Nothing happens in a city yard without it announcing the fact.

159.text: It poses as a dead branch. Its mournful night call unsettles travellers. It sits so still by day that hands pass right over it.

160.text: It eats snakes, rats and even small lambs. A symbol of the backlands. It walks the dry ground as often as it flies.

161.text: The largest bird of prey in the Americas. It takes monkeys and sloths. A single pair holds many square kilometres of forest.

162.text: It eats any rotting meat, and keeps the fields clean. It circles for hours on rising heat without one wingbeat.

163.text: Its eyes turn 270 degrees. It sees in total darkness. It hunts the forest floor from a low branch all night.

164.text: It nests in burrows in the savanna floor and flies in complete silence. It stands at the burrow mouth by day, watching everything.

165.text: It flies in flocks of hundreds, spearing fish with a bill like a sword. The flock works a drying pool until nothing is left in it.

166.text: The largest bird in the land. It flees at 60 km/h. The male raises the chicks of several females at once.

167.text: It beats venomous snakes against the ground until they die, then eats. It would far rather run than fly, and it runs very fast.

168.text: It lives in noisy bands, eating ticks off the backs of cattle. Several females share one nest and raise the brood together.

169.text: Its song carries so strongly that trainers compete over its tone. Its beak cracks seeds that would break a finger.

170.text: An elaborate song full of trills. The most prized bird in singing contests. A young one learns its song from the bird in the next cage.

171.text: A glittering blue that catches the sun. It eats fruit in gardens. Pairs raid the same fruit tree every morning without fail.

172.text: It eats army ants and nothing else, following the swarms for days. It goes hungry for days whenever the swarm goes quiet.

173.text: It lives in the low shade, startling butterflies with a beat of its wings. Pairs call to each other constantly to keep in contact.

174.text: It flies low after insects, its huge mouth opening in mid-air. It rests on the warm road at night and is easily missed.

175.text: It builds a mud nest shaped like an oven, a fixture of country yards. The nest takes two thousand trips to build, and lasts years.

176.text: A great-tree seed that has learned to walk on two roots. It walks until it finds good ground, then never moves again.

177.text: A sapling with sun-catching leaves. It waters itself in the rain. It turns to face the sun all day without being told.

178.text: A walking century-old tree. It stands still far more than it moves. A hundred creatures live in it and never notice it move.

179.text: A natural cup that gathers rainwater. Frogs live inside it all year round. It clings high in the branches, far above any puddle.

180.text: Its petals shimmer in every colour at once. The scent draws pollinators from kilometres away.

181.text: Its leaf is as wide as a double bed. It can hold a standing child without sinking.

182.text: It drops every leaf, then blooms bright yellow in the middle of the dry winter. A whole hillside of them flowers on the very same day.

183.text: It coils around trees and strangles them. A single one can wrap right around a hill.

184.text: Its heart is a prized delicacy, so it defends itself with thorns all along its trunk.

185.text: Its coconut is brutally hard. Only the strongest jaws in Arauna can crack one open.

186.text: It grows only where fresh water hides underground, marking out oases in the savanna.

187.text: A fruit that walks. The nut on its head bobs about like a little quiff. It hops between the dry thickets, always in a hurry.

188.text: It roasts its own nut in the scrubland sun. The aroma is impossible to ignore. One old tree of them can shade an entire village square.

189.text: A dark purple bunch crowns its head. Fighters swear by it for natural energy. Climbers go up thirty metres of bare trunk to reach it.

190.text: A yellow pod full of sweet seeds. Fermenting those seeds is what makes it evolve.

191.text: Its pods turn purple when ripe. Every bar of chocolate in Arauna begins here. It grows only in the shade of taller rainforest trees.

192.text: Its jet black seed looks like a staring eye. Pure natural energy, nothing added. The river villages have traded its seed for centuries.

193.text: Its bitter leaves are brewed into a shared drink, the companion of Arauna's herders.

194.text: Its ears come in yellow, red and purple. It feeds the villages through the year. Each village keeps its own seed, saved for generations.

195.text: Its long root looks like a leg. It buries itself whenever it wants to sleep.

196.text: A stone rolled smooth over thousands of years. Not one rough edge is left on it. It sits in the shallows and lets the current keep polishing.

197.text: A walking rock that rumbles as it rolls. The ground shakes wherever it passes. It rolls off the tableland cliffs and spends days climbing back.

198.text: A clear crystal. It grows one centimetre a year in the damp air of deep caves. A large one has been growing since before the first villages.

199.text: A glowing purple geode. It splits sunlight into rainbows across the cave walls.

200.text: A walking nugget of gold. Bandits chase it across the whole of Arauna. It hides in the hill streams, and it knows it is hunted.

201.text: A staggeringly heavy rock. It can only stand upright by planting its roots first.

202.text: The most precious stone of all. It throws rainbows in any light at all. Only a handful have ever been found in the Arauna hills.

203.text: Terracotta coloured. It sheds its skin in thin metallic plates as it grows. The plates it sheds litter the red earth all around it.

204.text: Glossy black. It swallows the light around it and gives none of it back. Stand near it and the whole hillside seems to dim.

205.text: It crystallises by itself in salt flats. It tastes sweet and bitter at once. The coastal salt pans are covered in them after a dry week.

206.text: It smells of rotten eggs. It grows in the fumaroles of volcanic ground. It gathers where the ground is too hot to stand on.

207.text: It moulds itself into any shape. A child's play is enough to change it for good.

208.text: Clay brought to life by children's games. It keeps every memory they gave it.

209.text: It grows one drop a century. Call it a stalagmite and it takes deep offence. Cave guides count the drips to guess how old it is.

210.text: It grows pointing upward. It has never once got along with stalactites. The two meet in the middle after a few thousand years.

211.text: A dinosaur bone that started walking again. Nobody can explain how. It walks the tableland at night looking for the rest of itself.

212.text: It fell from the sky thousands of years ago and is still warm to the touch. The crater it made is still bare after all that time.

213.text: Formed in an ancient eruption. It holds on to its heat for centuries. Frost melts in a wide ring around wherever it rests.

214.text: A classical statue brought to life by magic. Impeccably elegant about it. It corrects its own pose whenever it thinks nobody is watching.

215.text: The natural cracks across its body settle into angry looking faces. No two of them ever wear quite the same expression.

216.text: A hopping baby crab. Its claw already nips at unwary fingers. Thousands hatch on one tide and scatter across the sand.

217.text: It lives in burrows in the mangroves and comes out at night in great crowds. Whole stretches of mangrove get up and move on a full moon.

218.text: It swims sideways. Its bright blue claws flash under the shallow water. It buries itself in the sand with only its eyes showing.

219.text: It swims in pink shoals. Delicious grilled, or so the tourists say. It cleans the reef, picking parasites off larger fish.

220.text: It changes colour to match the seabed, and squirts ink when startled. It squeezes through a gap no wider than its own eye.

221.text: Its eight arms solve puzzles. It can open a jar with a screw lid. Divers say it remembers a face it has seen before.

222.text: Its stinging tentacles trail for metres. It drifts wherever the current goes. Whole fleets of them wash up on the beaches after a storm.

223.text: The male carries the young and raises them. It swims standing upright. It anchors its tail to a weed so the current cannot take it.

224.text: It hatches on the beach and runs for the sea on instinct alone. Terribly fragile. Of a hundred that hatch, perhaps one reaches full size.

225.text: It lives a hundred years, then returns to the beach it hatched on to lay eggs. It crosses whole oceans and still finds the exact beach.

226.text: It leaps in spinning arcs. It talks to its pod in sharp little clicks. The pod herds fish into a ring and takes turns feeding.

227.text: Its songs travel across whole oceans. It migrates with the seasons. Whole coastal villages gather on the cliffs to watch it pass.

228.text: It is born already swimming and hunting. It never has a childhood. Its mother is long gone before it is even born.

229.text: King of the sea. Its serrated teeth grow back for ever, however many it loses. It never truly sleeps, and it never stops swimming.

230.text: It hides in the sand of the seabed. Its shock stuns careless bathers. Beachgoers learn to shuffle their feet instead of stepping.

231.text: Its snout is shaped like a sword and can pierce the hull of a boat. It slashes through a shoal, then eats what it has stunned.

232.text: Its red scales blaze in the sun. Huge shoals gather over the reefs. A whole reef turns red when the shoal passes over it.

233.text: The glowing lure on its antenna fools smaller fish into swimming closer. It lives so deep that no sunlight has ever reached it.

234.text: It appears in school mirrors at night, calling out its own name. Children dare each other to say its name three times.

235.text: It steals children who refuse to sleep. It is not always real. Every village tells the story slightly differently.

236.text: It lives under beds. It frightens only children who disobey. It has never once been seen by an adult.

237.text: A seventh son under a full moon. Its howl sends every dog running. By morning it remembers nothing at all of the night.

238.text: A soul so wicked that even the earth refuses it. It wanders for ever. Not even the grave will hold it for a single night.

239.text: A giant hairy hand that reaches out from under the bed to grab at feet. It only reaches for feet left outside the blanket.

240.text: A hairy leg that walks alone at night, following anyone out on their own. It matches its step to whoever it is following.

241.text: The spirit of a woman who died in childbirth. It carries off babies. It leaves a scattering of flowers wherever it has passed.

242.text: Protector of the animals. It curses hunters who take more than they need. It takes the shape of a white deer to lead them astray.

243.text: The Tupi god of night. Only men are permitted to look upon its face. Its flutes are played at night and never shown by day.

244.text: The supreme Tupi-Guarani god. It looses lightning with a single blink. Every storm over the hills is said to be its work.

245.text: Goddess of the moon. Its silver hair shines on nights of the full moon. The tides and the planting calendar both answer to it.

246.text: God of the sun. Its golden crown lights the whole of Arauna. It set the first fire and handed it to the people.

247.text: God of love. Its arrow of flowers brings two hearts together. It travels as a wind carrying messages between lovers.

248.text: The spirit of fermented drink. It brightens festivals and healing rites. It turns up wherever the drums and the drink both run late.

249.text: Its black dye lasts for weeks on skin. Elders paint blessings with it. The patterns it paints say who a person is to the village.

250.text: An ancestral red dye. It keeps biting insects away for a whole day. Hunters paint their faces with it before setting out.

251.text: It rides a wild boar. It guards the game and runs down greedy hunters. Leave tobacco at the treeline and it will let you pass.

252.text: The red form the forest protector takes when its anger finally boils over. The whole forest falls silent when it takes that shape.

253.text: The river spirit in the shape of an angler. It teaches the young to respect the water.

254.text: It treads on the chest of anyone who sleeps on a full stomach, freezing them. It waits up on the roof beams until the lamps go out.

255.text: The spirit of a quilombo leader. It stirs courage in all who fight for freedom.

256.text: The young form of the sea goddess. It rules over the smaller tides. Children leave it flowers at the water's edge.

257.text: It commands the power of healing leaves. Any poison gives way before it. It knows the use of every leaf in the coastal forest.

258.text: A creator spirit dressed all in white. It blesses everyone who comes near. Nothing it touches can ever be made unclean again.

259.text: A young trickster. It cannot control its whirlwinds properly yet. It practises on the dust of the road and knocks itself over.

260.text: Red cap, pipe and a single leg. It turns up all across Arauna's folklore. Trap it in a bottle and it will bargain for its freedom.

261.text: An elder forest guardian. It knows where every ancestral tree still grows. Its feet point backwards, so its trail leads the wrong way.

262.text: Another form of the keeper of the game, and even harder on greedy hunters. It counts what a hunter takes and remembers every one.

263.text: An alluring spirit. Its laughter rings out at the crossroads after dark. Offerings are left for it at midnight, never any earlier.

264.text: Keeper of the crossroads. Nothing gets past it without its say so. It is greeted first at every ceremony, without exception.

265.text: An ancestral spirit. It smokes a pipe and gives advice a thousand years old. People come from three towns over just to sit with it.

266.text: A spectral native warrior wearing a headdress of brightly coloured feathers. It appears where the old forest paths are still walked.

267.text: The spirit of a drowned sailor. It tells stories of storms all night long. It sits on the harbour wall and no boat leaves while it talks.

268.text: A festival spirit. It plays the berimbau and never once stops. Every coastal festival is louder for its being there.

269.text: The spirit of a famous outlaw, in a leather hat studded with silver stars. It still rides the backland roads its band once held.

270.text: The spirit of a beloved priest. It blesses with a rosary of cactus beads. Pilgrims walk for days to reach the place it appears.

271.text: The spirit of an innocent child. It appears at the epiphany parades. It leads the procession, and nobody sees it arrive.

272.text: King of carnival. Its throne is built entirely out of glitter. The city hands it the keys for four days every year.

273.text: The spirit of the festival ox. It comes back to life at every performance. The crowd shouts it back to its feet every single time.

274.text: The spirit of the epiphany dance. Its accordion plays all on its own. It goes from door to door and is never turned away.

275.text: The spirit of the frevo. Its acrobatic dance simply never stops. Its little umbrella spins the whole time it is in the air.

276.text: A spectral royal parade in a golden crown and embroidered robes. The whole parade moves to one drum, and it leads.

277.text: A warrior spirit in procession. Its staves beat out a steady rhythm. The rhythm is older than any village that still keeps it.

278.text: A spirit that travels from party to party. It never tires of dancing. It has not missed a carnival in living memory.

279.text: A legendary black jaguar, worshipped as a goddess of the night forest. It is only ever seen as a shadow crossing a clearing.

280.text: An anaconda ten metres long. It swallows capybaras whole. After a large meal it does not move for a month.

281.text: The king of the river fish. Five metres long, in scales like armour plate. The oldest river people say it remembers the first flood.

282.text: Alpha of the legendary pack. Its fire burns a greenish turquoise. The rest of the pack will not eat until it has.

283.text: The enormous queen of its kind. It commands whole swarms at a word. It has never once left the marsh where it hatched.

284.text: A bird a century old. Its beak carved out entire tablelands. Every canyon in the tableland is a mark it left.

285.text: The primordial fire serpent. Its blue flame devours whole woods. It comes only after a fire, and comes for whoever set it.

286.text: Mother of all the river spirits. Its song is heard once in a lifetime. Whoever hears it never speaks of it afterwards.

287.text: King of the forest guardians. Its hair burns the red of urucum dye. No axe has ever been raised in the grove it protects.

288.text: The ancestral trickster. Its red cap is a legend in its own right. Every whirlwind on every road in Arauna answers to it.

289.text: The supreme forest protector. White deer follow wherever it goes. The herd that follows it has been counted at a thousand.

290.text: An Amazonian love turned into a living tree. Its wood is carved into charms that are given, never sold.

291.text: A serpent man. It takes human shape only during the festivals. It leaves its skin on the riverbank while it dances.

292.text: A primordial giant sloth. A mouth in its chest, and the smell of death. Whole expeditions have turned back at the smell alone.

293.text: A man-eating fish man. The terror of the fishermen of old. The old charts still mark the bays it was seen in.

294.text: A legendary bird. The whole forest falls silent the moment it sings. It sings for a few minutes a year, and no longer.

295.text: A jade green charm of the warrior women. It brings luck in battle. It is buried with its owner and dug up by the next.

296.text: An archer queen of a legendary tribe. Its bow stands taller than a person. It leads a tribe that no map has ever managed to place.

297.text: An ancient peak. Old growth forest covers the whole of its back. Rivers begin on its shoulders and never run dry.

298.text: A spirit with open arms. It blesses all who watch the sun come up. It stands where the first light reaches the hills.

299.text: It lives in the sewers and will eat absolutely anything it finds. It knows the sewer network better than any engineer.

300.text: It tears open rubbish bags. Its droppings ruin every statue in town. Feed it once and it never leaves your balcony again.

301.text: An enormous pigeon. It rules entire town squares all by itself. It has learned exactly which benches people eat on.

302.text: A flying roach out of a nightmare. It aims straight at whoever screams. It only ever flies when it is least welcome.

303.text: A striped little streak of a thing. It carries disease from town to town. A single cup of standing water breeds hundreds of them.

304.text: The wild counterpart of the caramel pup. It defends its turf in packs. It belonged to somebody once, and it has not forgotten.

305.text: They say it is bad luck if it crosses your path. So they say. It has heard the story, and it seems to enjoy it.

306.text: It turns up in toilet bowls and leaps at the face of whoever sits down. It comes up through the pipes after heavy rain.

307.text: It eats mosquitoes. Its tail drops off and keeps wriggling by itself. Every kitchen wall in Arauna has one watching the lamp.

308.text: It eats old paper, and soaks up the knowledge of the books it ruins. Librarians have given up and now leave it a shelf of its own.

309.text: A walking ball of dust. It grows larger in every closed up room. Open a shut up house and it rolls out to meet you.

310.text: It eats metal from the inside out. Bridges give way without warning. By the time it shows on the surface it is far too late.

311.text: A cloud of exhaust fumes. It darkens the sky over the cities. It thickens over the city every evening at the same hour.

312.text: A spill of leaked oil. It kills every sea creature it drifts across. A beach it reaches takes twenty years to recover.

313.text: A living heap of city rubbish. Heavy rain is what makes it evolve. It grows every night, and nobody remembers building it.

314.text: The black liquid that seeps out of a rubbish heap. It poisons all it touches. Nothing grows again in ground it has run through.

315.text: It is still burning when thrown away, and sets whole pastures alight. One thrown from a car window can burn a whole hillside.

316.text: It roams about looking for another of its kind to scrap with. Turn it in for recycling and it pays you for the trouble.

317.text: It flies on the wind and snags in the trees for decades on end. There are trees in Arauna wearing them like old flags.

318.text: It floats down the rivers and drifts all the way out to the open sea. It has been floating longer than most towns it drifts past.

319.text: A bird made of the plastic in its own stomach. A symbol of pollution. Its own parents fed it that until it could no longer fly.

320.text: It leaks corrosive acid. It should never, ever be picked up. Bury one and it poisons the well for the whole street.

321.text: A tangle of live electrical wire. A walking short circuit. It hangs over the street where the poles have given up.

322.text: A giant urban bug. It shows up in kitchens nobody bothers to clean. It has been living behind the fridge for years.

323.text: A folded sheet of kitchen foil. It flies on the wind like a kite. It comes back down and folds itself flat again.

324.text: A broken chunk of pavement. It trips people up on purpose. The same slab has caught the same people for years.

325.text: The spirit of waste water. It rises out of the drains in a flood. It rises to street level with the first heavy rain.

326.text: A traffic light that changes for no reason at all, snarling up the roads. Drivers have learned to ignore whatever it tells them.

327.text: A street lamp that walks. It lights up the darkest streets in town. It follows the last person home, then goes out.

328.text: The spirit of street art. Its shape changes with whatever it paints. Paint over it and it comes back larger by morning.

329.text: Consort of the sun god. It shines brightest at first light. It rises a moment before the sun does, every single day.

330.text: Consort of the moon goddess. It shines brightest at midnight. It keeps the count of the months for the whole region.

331.text: The thunder god in primordial form. One clap levels a hillside. The oldest hills in Arauna still carry the scars.

332.text: The river spirit at its height. A whole river obeys its song. Every tributary changes course when it decides so.

333.text: The sun of the first days. It gave life to the entire continent. The first people of Arauna were shaped in its light.

334.text: The moon of the first days. It rules the tides and dreams alike. It and the sun of the first days have never once met.

335.text: Love in its very first form. It brings destined couples together. It loosed the arrow before there was anyone to hit.

336.text: The spirit of a whole river basin. One body, a thousand tributaries. Cut off one arm of it and another opens somewhere else.

337.text: Supreme guardian of the region. It appears only when Arauna is in danger. It has woken three times in all of recorded history.

338.text: The spirit of the primordial rainforest. It sprouts from the ashes of fires. Every burned clearing in Arauna is watched over by it.

339.text: The spirit of the December rains. It soaks Arauna through in three days. The whole region plants the day after it passes.

340.text: The spirit of the dry season. It scorches the fields for months on end. It sleeps under the cracked ground until the rains fail.

341.text: The southern wind that brings the winter cold, whistling deadly tunes. It arrives from the south overnight and turns the air cold.

342.text: Walking fertile soil. A crop springs up wherever it sets foot. Farmers set food out on the tableland hoping it will pass.

343.text: The primordial fire that first warmed Arauna at the beginning. It has burned in the same place since the beginning.

344.text: The spirit of the Atlantic. The waves keep time to its rhythm. Every tide along the coast is counted out by it.

345.text: The spirit of daybreak. A rose and gold light fills the whole sky. It and the spirit of sunset never see one another.

346.text: The spirit of sunset. Burnt colours at the close of the afternoon. It waits all day at the far edge of the water.

347.text: A shooting star that made a nest here. It grants the wishes made on it. It has been in the same hillside hollow for centuries.

348.text: The whole region made flesh. There is only ever one of it. Nobody has proved it exists, and nobody has proved otherwise.

349.text: It screams at dawn to warn the flock. The forest's own alarm clock. The whole flock takes up the cry until the danger passes.

350.text: It howls at daybreak. Its call marks its turf for kilometres around. A troop calls at dawn, and again just before rain.

351.text: The smallest parrot in Arauna. It flies in loud green flocks. A flock of forty fits into a single hollow branch.

352.text: A clever parrot. It mimics human voices to throw predators off. It has learned the calls of the hawks that hunt it.

353.text: A blue macaw with a hooked beak. Its pairs stay together for life. A pair that loses one partner never takes another.

354.text: A shy, round eyed rodent. It lives in burrows out in the grassland. It bolts for the nearest burrow at the smallest sound.

355.text: The largest rodent in the world. Birds and monkeys ride about on it. Whole families doze at the water's edge every afternoon.

356.text: It rides on its mother's back until it is grown, licking up ants all day. It hangs by its tail from a low branch to sleep.

357.text: Its sticky tongue is sixty centimetres long. It smells a nest kilometres off. It has no teeth at all, and has never needed any.

358.text: Its front claws are enormous. It scares off jaguars standing on its hind legs. It backs against a mound and dares anything to come on.

359.text: It moves so slowly that moss grows all over its fur. Its own coat is a small forest of algae and moths.

360.text: It sleeps twenty hours a day. Its dreams change the weather around it. It comes down from its tree once a week, no oftener.

361.text: It beats its wings eighty times a second and drinks nectar in mid air. It visits two thousand flowers in a single day.

362.text: Its feathers scatter sunlight into shifting bands of colour. Its colour changes entirely depending where you stand.

363.text: The core in its chest holds a spark taken from the sun itself. It is seen only at the exact moment of sunrise.

364.text: Its curls are golden. It brings luck to anyone fishing nearby. It sits on the rocks combing them out for hours.

365.text: It sways without ever stopping, and kicks in the middle of the dance. It has never once thrown the first strike.

366.text: A living gourd that plays itself. It sets the rhythm of the circle. The whole circle stops the moment that it does.

367.text: Every beat shakes the ground. It keeps time for the whole ceremony. Three of them together can be heard across a city.

368.text: It spins on the spot, playing a samba all by itself. It knows every rhythm and refuses to play the easy ones.

369.text: It breathes out tunes that make anyone listening weep with longing. It plays the backland squares until well past midnight.

370.text: A walking country guitar. It sings ballads out of very old tales. Every ballad it sings actually happened to somebody.

371.text: A deep drum that leads the dance. Hearts start beating in time with it. The dance does not begin until it says so.

372.text: A chapbook of verse that reads itself out loud to anyone passing. It hangs itself on a string in the market and waits.

373.text: It weaves invisible lace that catches bad dreams before they land. Coastal families hang its lace above the cradle.

374.text: Its skin is covered in sharp scales. Fishermen give it a wide berth. It takes a hook and simply keeps swimming with it.

375.text: It swims in shoals of dozens. Together they strip a cow in minutes. Most of the year it eats fruit and bothers nobody.

376.text: A fire snake that punishes anyone who burns the forest. Eyes like embers. It rolls through the burnt ground counting what was lost.

377.text: An ancestral river king. One flick of its tail empties a whole lake. The lake it left is now a stretch of open savanna.

378.text: An ancient turtle. Its shell hides a forest in miniature. It has not moved from the same bend in the river in an age.

379.text: Its body is a living sphere of sun. Stars go out when it appears. It cannot go near the moon spirit without one of them fading.

380.text: Its body is a silver crescent moon. It rules the tides and dreams. It draws the whole ocean after it, night after night.

381.text: A king of Palmares reborn. A symbol of freedom across Arauna. Its name is still shouted at the head of every march.

382.text: Queen of the sea. Offerings are carried to it every February. Whole cities go down to the beach with flowers for it.

383.text: A rainbow serpent. It bridges earth and sky in a band of colour. It spends half the year in the sky and half underground.

384.text: A forest guardian's young in its first form. Only pure children see it. Its footprints already point the wrong way round.

385.text: A newborn trickster. Little whirlwinds spin up wherever it goes. It has the cap and the pipe and no idea what to do with either.

386.text: The first creature of Arauna. It holds the essence of the whole region. Everything else in the region came out of it.
